# The owner's standing rules

These outrank a good-looking frame. They came from the project owner one at a time, after something
went wrong, and the reason is written beside each one so nobody repeals it later for looking fussy.

*(Markers are defined in [`../../ENGINE-CHECK.md`](../../ENGINE-CHECK.md), which owns the set and the rule that each one closes two ways — resolved, or `unobtainable`, with what was done instead.)*

## Which of these apply to the piece in front of you

**None of these rules stops the work, and none is a matter of rights, permission or taste.** They
describe how the owner likes his own heritage work made. Where a rule meets something missing or in
conflict, the working rule in the root `SKILL.md` §0 settles it: the brief, the skill, the web, then
the most suitable choice, recorded and carried on.

**Part A applies to the owner's own work.** On anyone else's project the brief governs, and a Part A
rule applies only where the brief asks for it. The one exception is rule 3's *No twins*: it is a property
of the generator rather than a preference, so it holds on every project.

**Part B applies only to a history piece the user wants realistic** — the ancient world, or the
Assyrian, Chaldean and Syriac story, made to look the way it does on the reliefs and in the museums.
It governs the historical frames only: a present-day setting in the same piece — a client's shop, a
street, a family kitchen — is shown as the brief wants it. On a stylised, decorative or playful piece
(a small lamassu as decoration, a coloured cartoon Nineveh) the brief decides the look, not these rules.

# Part A — the owner's work and heritage projects

---

## 1. A reference for each historical element, when the piece wants it real

On a realistic history piece, look for a reference for each historical element — a relief, a gate, a
lamassu, a king, a garment: first in the canon, then on the web. **Found, attach it. Not found, generate
the closest thing and carry on.** It is never a condition: no marker, no licence step, no waiting.

The one filter is story relevance: only people and things tied to this story go in the reference
folder. Background extras — a crowd, workers, soldiers — are fine where the shot calls for them.

## 2. Flags belong to the period, and a flag is a modern object

A national flag is a rectangle of coloured cloth standing for a state, and it is a modern
invention. Whichever flag a scene calls for, it is built from a real reference like every other
historical element, and it appears because the scene genuinely contains it — a building, a stadium,
an office, a street — never as background decoration or for visual variety.

**On a pre-330 BC subject there are no flags at all.** What an ancient army or procession carries is
a **standard** — a pole with a cast or carved emblem at the head, not a banner. Build it from the
canon and from a real reference the same way every other historical element is built:

- **Assyrian** — the winged sun disc. In the Middle Assyrian period it carries the upper torso of the
  god Ashur holding a drawn bow (`grimoire-12-middle-assyrian.md`, heading 6); by the Neo-Assyrian
  period it is Ashur hovering in the disc above the king, and the canon does not give him the bow
  there (`grimoire-16-neo-assyrian.md`, heading 6). Take whichever the period gives. Bull and lion
  emblems sit on the pole head.
- **Babylonian** — the mushussu, Marduk's dragon, and the eight-pointed star of Ishtar.
- **Persian, after the Assyrian fall** — the Faravahar disc.

Writing "banners" or "flags" into a prompt for an ancient scene is how a modern rectangle of cloth
ends up in a seventh-century BC frame. Name the standard and its emblem instead, and attach the
reference.

## 3. Faces in a generated set

**No twins.** A character set generated in one batch comes back as brothers with one face. Vary age,
build, nose, hairline and beard **per character, explicitly**, and review the set as a set before it
goes anywhere. This is a property of the generator, not of a subject, so it holds on any project.

**A real living person needs an identity reference, not a description.** Writing a public figure's
name or describing their face in words produces a stranger who resembles them. If the piece needs
them, supply the likeness properly — a trained identity, a reference image the model accepts — and
if that is not available, stage the shot from behind or off the face. Choose the tool that can hold
the likeness rather than avoiding the shot.

**Where the brief says no faces at all**, the staging craft is `ai.hidden_faces` (from behind, in
silhouette, under a headdress, with the hands carrying the beat). It hides a face nobody can know; it
does not protect a living person who must not be identified, which `doc.anonymous_interview` hands over.

**Look up a real historical figure's documented appearance when designing them**: the Vita, the
chronicler, the surviving icons, first in the canon, then on the web. Found, use it; nothing found, design
the closest thing the period supports. Write what you found, or chose, into the project folder. Two figures were
once invented from nothing and he caught both.

## 4. Never invent a religious detail

Where a piece does carry religious material, look each element up (the canon, then the web) and draw
what the record shows.
A Latin-style shaved tonsure on Syriac monks read to him as mockery, and was historically wrong as
well. If a detail is not documented, leave it neutral rather than plausible.

## 5. Subtitles and lyrics are burned in the edit, never generated

Not on any generated image, not on any generated video frame. Subtitles and lyrics are a delivery layer added in the post-production edit. (Note: Storyboard pitch decks are explicitly exempt as presentation/pitch artifacts, not delivered production frames).

## 6. Sheets

- **A character sheet is the person and the costume only.** No prop in the hand, no staging, no
  scene. Props get their own sheet. **A sheet is not a keyframe.**
- **The layout is fixed** and it is in `../sheet-character.md`: four full-body views - front, back,
  left side, right side - plus **four face close-ups**: neutral front, a **smile showing the teeth**,
  three-quarter left, three-quarter right.
- **The teeth smile is the important one.** Teeth are where generated faces break - shape, count,
  colour, gum line - and a sheet without a smile gives the model nothing to hold onto the first time
  the character smiles. Every later shot inherits that gap.

## 7. Cost, and checking the engine before you rely on it

- **The engine's real limits are checked when the project starts, not remembered.** Clip length,
  whether an end frame is accepted at the resolution you are using, what an account's unlimited tier
  actually covers and whether it applies through the route you are calling. These change every few
  months and a remembered limit is how a shot gets designed around a restriction that no longer
  exists — or breaks on one that has appeared.
- **Where an unlimited tier exists it is usually account-level**, and calling the same model through
  a different route can draw credits instead. Confirm which route the run will use before it runs.
- **Prefer the cheaper resolution** while the shot is still being proven, and raise it once the frame
  is approved.
- Keep the work in a Space or a named folder.

## 8. Two rules about him, not about the frame

Both apply to the owner's own runs only, not to a client's project.

- **Announce before generating.** Say what is about to run; his go-ahead is the spend approval
  (`paid_generation_approved_by`), and this rule adds no other wait. He has his own plan for how to
  run it.
- **Report every generation with an info card:** the model and its settings, how many references and
  their names, the cost in credits, the job id, and the remaining balance. He tracks the spend
  himself.

# Part B — Mesopotamian and Assyrian heritage pieces only

These are about a subject. On a piece that is not about that subject they do not apply at all, and
applying them anyway takes away things the work needs.

---

## 9. People must read Assyrian and Mesopotamian

The face, the hair, the beard, the build. For an ancient subject that means the iconic
curled-and-braided long hair and the square ringleted beards, the strong distinct features, the
physique in the reliefs. **A generic "Middle Eastern" face is a failure.** The canon's face is the
elite's; a working person takes the same features with the grooming and dress of the trade (grimoire-16,
heading 3).

**Cast from the right millennium.** For a **late-antique Christian** subject — Nisibis, the Syriac
world of AD 350 to 600 — the Neo-Assyrian reliefs are the wrong evidence entirely. Cast from
photographs of Assyrian, Chaldean and Syriac people instead.

## 10. Religious imagery follows the brief

**The skill adds no religious symbol and removes none on its own.** Whether a cross, a veil, a
vestment, a prayer pose or any other religious sign appears is the brief's call, and the owner says
it in the request when it matters. What always holds is rule 4: nothing religious is invented, and
every religious element that does appear is looked up first, and one nothing documents is left neutral.

The one historical fact this touches is the head covering: Middle Assyrian law made a head-shawl
compulsory for the free wife and the betrothed, as a mark of legal standing, and Mesopotamia had no
face veil (rule 11, and Nos. 38 and 39 in `clothing-08-middle-assyrian.md`). A covering drawn across
the face in an ancient frame is therefore a modern choice, made only where the brief asks for it.

## 11. Head covering, the one historical correction

Middle Assyrian law §40 governs, and it is about a **head** covering, not a face veil. Mesopotamia
had no face veil. The detail is in `clothing-08-middle-assyrian.md`, under *Women, Age and the
Covering Law* (Nos. 38 to 59); take its wording.

## 12. Timeless, not occasion-bound

A heritage piece must read as eternal Mesopotamian and Iraqi heritage, not as tied to the month it
was made, so it still works in three years.

**This does not apply to a piece whose subject is the occasion.** A World Cup anthem, an anniversary
film, a piece made for a specific date — the occasion is what it is about, and hiding it would empty
it. The rule governs the heritage piece that merely happens to be published near a date.

## The checklist, before anything is sent

**Every piece Part A covers (see *Which of these apply* above)**

- [ ] On a realistic history piece: a reference found and attached for each historical element, or the closest thing generated
- [ ] Any flag present because the scene contains it, with a reference; no flags at all before 330 BC
- [ ] No two generated characters alike; a real person carried by an identity reference, not a description
- [ ] No invented religious detail
- [ ] No subtitle or lyric generated into a frame (burned in the edit); any other in-frame text keeps the treatment `in-frame-text.md` selected
- [ ] The engine's current limits checked, not remembered
- [ ] On the owner's own runs: announced, and the settings and cost ready to report (rule 8)

**Heritage pieces, additionally**

- [ ] Date checked. Is the canon open for this subject (pre-330 BC boundary in `canon-rules.md`)?
- [ ] Faces cast from the right millennium
- [ ] Nothing that dates the piece to this month, unless the occasion is the subject
